title: Ukraine's Largest Drone Maker: Nearly 100,000 a Month, AI Interception Is Just the First Step
dek: Ukrainian drone maker General Cherry produces nearly 100,000 drones a month, and its interceptor drones take down Russian Shaheds costing over $50,000 at a cost of about $2,000 each. AI guidance is already in combat, but full autonomy is still far off.
why: This episode is a rare case of a leading Ukrainian drone manufacturer describing directly the real shape of battlefield drones, their costs, and the boundaries of AI use. It is information-dense and directly valuable for understanding modern warfare and the drone industry.
who: Founders, investors and engineers watching the shape of modern warfare, the drone industry and military applications of AI.
skip: The company introduction at the start can be skipped; go straight to the middle and later sections on AI and cost.

points.h: Nearly 100,000 a month, and capacity is still expanding
points.body: General Cherry was founded in 2023 and initially produced only about 10 drones a month; today monthly output reaches about 100,000 (the exact figure is confidential). The company has worked with more than 110 military brigades, and its best units consume more than 5,000 drones a month. Capacity is still rising, because battlefield consumption is enormous and drones have become expendables.

points.h: Ukraine has hundreds of drone companies, but only 10-15 at the top
points.body: The number of drone companies in Ukraine may be as high as 2,000, but the vast majority are garage-scale workshops. Only 10 to 15 large companies can truly produce 1,000 to 10,000 drones a month, and General Cherry claims to be in the top five. This fragmented yet enormous industrial ecosystem is the foundation of Ukraine's rapid innovation, but it also means fierce competition.

points.h: AI models are built in-house, co-created deeply with the military
points.body: General Cherry's AI guidance system is entirely self-developed, backed by a strong R&D department, and built in close cooperation with different military units at the front. They gather battlefield feedback every day through mobile teams and iterate on products quickly. This ‘R&D-combat-feedback’ loop lets Ukrainian drone technology adapt rapidly to battlefield changes rather than relying on external procurement.

points.h: The rocket-shaped FPV came from Red Bull, not Ukraine
points.body: This rocket-shaped FPV drone is not a Ukrainian invention; Red Bull first used it in 2021 or 2022 for sporting events. Ukrainian companies found that this shape could reach higher speeds than ordinary quadcopters, so they adopted and optimised it. This reflects the rapid learning and pragmatism of Ukraine's drone industry — it does not chase originality, only effectiveness.

General Cherry's interceptor drones (such as Bullet) cost about $2,000 but can shoot down Russian Shahed drones that cost $50,000 to $100,000. This asymmetric cost exchange is Ukraine's key strategy for dealing with Russia's ‘saturation attacks’ — using cheap drones to drain the enemy's expensive assets while avoiding wasting the expensive air-defence missiles supplied by the West.

points.h: Interceptors have confirmed more than 5,000 Russian shootdowns
points.body: Since entering production in February 2025, General Cherry's tactical interceptor drone (General Trajectory Air) has confirmed more than 5,000 Russian drone shootdowns, including more than 1,000 Russian ‘Moniya’ drones in December alone. The model that intercepts Shaheds also entered mass production in December 2025, with confirmed shootdowns approaching 1,000. These numbers show that interceptor drones have become an important force in battlefield air defence.

points.h: AI runs on the device, not in the cloud
points.body: General Cherry's AI guidance model runs on the camera chip aboard the drone itself, not in the cloud. After an operator detects a target by radar and launches the drone, the AI automatically identifies and locks onto the target without human intervention. This on-device AI design avoids battlefield communication latency and jamming, and is the key to making it viable in real combat.

points.h: Fully autonomous weapons are a terrifying future, but AI is now unavoidable
points.body: Marko admits that if drones became fully autonomous it would be terrifying — killing would no longer require another person, only a robot or a drone. At present they use semi-autonomous AI only on interceptor drones, because adding AI to ordinary FPVs significantly raises the cost, and it is better to buy a few more without AI. But he predicts AI technology will spread quickly and prices will fall, making future battlefields even more brutal.
